source.title: Towards Better Generalization: Weight Decay Induces Low-rank Bias for Neural Networks
source.authors: Ke Chen; Chu-Gang Yi; Hai-Zhao Yang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments relating weight decay, stable rank, batch size, and generalization error, and derives generalization bounds from low-rank bias. These are related to the claim's conditions and measured properties, but it does not test the versions' specified natural-label memorization, width sweep, architecture comparison, optimizer comparison, large-batch penalty, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example removal.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own reported results on weight decay, batch size, stable rank, and generalization error. Theoretical results and cited findings are not separate empirical rows; accuracy curves without recoverable values are recorded as figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study tests weight decay's effect on stable rank and train–test gaps, rather than any listed version. Its batch sweeps use 4–32 or 8–64 examples without establishing a large-batch regime; approximately constant gaps do not establish constant held-out performance or test V5's large-batch penalty.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. More precisely, the authors prove approximate low rank assuming uniformly small batch gradients, and a tighter generalization bound assuming zero batch gradients and bounded outputs. Their experiments report smaller train–test discrepancies in selected stronger-weight-decay settings; these discrepancies should not be equated with improved held-out accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses two-layer ReLU networks with square loss, mini-batch SGD, conventional weight decay, and regression-style generalization error on California Housing and MNIST. It does not implement the claim versions' interventions or comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Weight-decay coefficient μV strongly changes stable rank and reported generalization outcomes; batch size has weak dependence in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing weight decay reduces stable rank on California Housing and MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stronger conventional weight decay can induce approximately rank-one first-layer weights in the tested two-layer ReLU networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected stronger-weight-decay settings yield smaller reported train–test gaps, despite increased training MSE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight decay can reduce train–test discrepancies in this setup; this alone does not establish better held-out performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Under strong weight decay, the authors report weak dependence of stable rank and train–test gaps on the tested batch sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stable rank and train–test discrepancies vary little over these small-batch sweeps.

fits_no_version.finding: Small gradients for every batch imply proximity to low-rank weights; zero batch gradients and bounded outputs yield a tighter generalization bound.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the stated assumptions, low-rank structure improves the parameter dependence of a theoretical generalization bound.

record.problems: The experiments use one architecture and square loss, including square loss for MNIST classification; numerical generalization-error and accuracy values are not stated in the prose. The experimental results are primarily conveyed in figures. The theoretical generalization bound assumes zero batch gradients, while the approximate low-rank result uses a small-gradient assumption.
record.rows_left_out: No required rows were omitted; figures include additional plotted trajectories and histograms, but individual numerical values are not stated in the text and are not needed as separate rows for tested claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width variation beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Held-out performance beyond a workload-dependent large-batch threshold under fixed epoch budgets, and whether recipe changes remove a penalty.
Dropout interventions, dataset-size dependence, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its relationship to generalization gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are assessed against the listed claim versions. None means the row is outside those versions, rather than evidence that its reported low-rank effect is absent.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label memorization or natural-label generalization comparison.
No width sweep past interpolation or test-error comparison.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD.
No large-batch penalty test under fixed epoch budgets.
Stable rank is measured, but magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the generalization gap are not tested.
